props.title: Tails, You Win
lines: A few extreme outcomes drive most of finance. Being wrong often can still win.
Index-like patience is how you make sure you own the tail.

props.title: More than 21,000 financings, 2004–2014

rows.v: 65% of venture financings lost money.
Two and a half percent made ten times to twenty times.
One percent made more than a twenty-times return.
Half a percent — about 100 companies out of 21,000 — earned 50× or more. That is where most industry returns come from.

props.note: Correlation Ventures, as cited in the book.

props.title: Russell 3000 since 1980 (J.P. Morgan A.M., as cited)

rows.v: 40% of Russell 3000 components lost at least 70% of their value and never recovered.
Effectively all of the index's overall returns came from 7% of companies that outperformed by at least two standard deviations.
1926–2016: the best-performing about 4% of listed companies explain the net gain of the entire U.S. stock market; the rest collectively matched Treasury bills.
Amazon drove about 6% of S&P 500 returns in 2018. Apple: almost 7%.

props.kicker: ONE TAIL CAN PAY THE REST
props.title: Snow White versus hundreds of shorts

rows.v: Disney's first studio went bankrupt. By the mid-1930s he had produced more than 400 cartoons; most lost money.
The $8 million earned in the first six months of 1938 dwarfed anything before. Debts paid. New Burbank studio. Celebrity.
By 1938 he had produced several hundred hours of film. In business terms, the 83 minutes of Snow White were what mattered.
Berggruen-style dealers bought portfolios. Perhaps 99% of works were of little value if 1% was Picasso.

props.kicker: STAYING IN FOR THE TAIL MONTHS
props.title: $1 a month, 1900–2019

rows.v: Invests $1 every month, rain or shine. Ends with $435,551.
Sells in recessions, holds cash, buys back after. Ends with $257,386.
Sells six months after a recession starts, buys six months after it ends. Ends with $234,476.
1,428 months in the span; just over 300 were recession months — about 22% of the time. Sue's cool there is most of the gap.
How you behaved in a few months of late 2008 and early 2009 can outweigh everything from 2000 to 2008.

props.title: Failure is not a glitch in the system

rows.v: Most venture deals lose money. That is the design, not an accident.
Forty percent of Russell 3000 names lost 70% and never recovered — inside a 'boring' index.
Bessembinder's about 4% of listed firms, and J.P. Morgan's 7% of the Russell, are why diversification exists.
Missing the ugly 22% of months cost Jim and Tom roughly 40% of Sue's pile.
Your job is to still be invested when the handful of winners show up.

props.title: Stay for the handful
items: Most venture deals lose money. That is how the industry is built, not a scandal.
Forty percent of Russell three thousand names lost seventy percent and never recovered, inside a boring index.
Sue captured the ugly months. Jim and Tom did not. The pile gap is the point.
Your job is not to be right every year. It is to still be invested when the few winners arrive.
